newsitem.title: USA: Jury deliberations begin in Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury deliberations begin in Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: Jurors began weighing the fate of Oklahoma City bombing defendant Timothy McVeigh on Friday after being warned by the judge not to be swayed by sympathy or by public opinion.

The seven men and five women went to the jury room to select a foreperson at 9:33 a.m. (1533 GMT). The six alternate jurors were sent to a separate room. The jurors, who had been free to go home at nights, have now been sequestered.

"You will retire and begin your deliberations in this case," federal Judge Richard Matsch said after giving the jury final instructions on the law and how they must treat evidence in the emotionally charged case.

McVeigh, 29, a decorated Gulf War veteran, is accused of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people in the worst attack on civilians in U.S. history. He has pleaded not guilty and could face the death penalty if convicted.

McVeigh, usually expressionless, frowned occasionally as he watched the judge read his instructions to the packed courtroom. The jurors paid close attention as Matsch told them they must not be swayed by public opinion or by sympathy.

"You are to be guided solely by the evidence in this case," he said. He told them they should find McVeigh guilty if they were convinced by the evidence against him, even if they thought others were involved in the alleged plot.

But if they had a reasonable doubt "you should not hesitate to return a verdict of not guilty," Matsch said. "The question can never be will the government win or lose this case. The government always wins when justice is done regardless of whether the verdict is guilty or not guilty."
The government is under intense pressure to win a conviction because of public outrage over the bombing.
Chief defence attorney Stephen Jones said he had spoken with McVeigh after the case went to the jury. "He's feeling good, I don't think he is nervous," he told reporters.

Marsha Kight, whose 23-year-old daughter Frankie Merrell died in the blast, told reporters she had been on an emotional roller-coaster. "Right now I have a lot of anxiety, a feeling of powerlessness," she said.

She said she thought McVeigh looked rather sombre. "He's really hard to read. Most of the time he looks real stoic," added Kight, one of a number of victims' relatives who have followed court proceedings.
Matsch also told the jurors they must scrutinise the testimony of three key prosecution witnesses with great care because they may have had a motive to lie.

McVeigh's former army buddy Michael Fortier, who testified that McVeigh told him in advance of his plans to blow up the federal building, reached a plea bargain agreement with the government on bombing-related charges. McVeigh's sister Jennifer and Fortier's wife Lori both testified against McVeigh under a grant of immunity from prosecution.

Matsch said the fact McVeigh chose not to testify in his own defence should not play a part in jury deliberations. He described the charges against McVeigh, who is accused of conspiracy to detonate a bomb, two bombing charges and eight murder counts for eight federal agents killed in the blast.

The prosecution alleges McVeigh is an extreme right-winger driven by his hatred of the U.S. government to blow up the federal building, while the defence maintains the government has the wrong man and that the real bomber died in the blast.

The trial has gone much faster than expected, pushed forward by Matsch, a no-nonsense judge. Jury selection began on March 31 and opening arguments were on April 24. The prosecution called 137 witnesses over 18 days while the defence called 25 witnesses over four days.
Prosecutors said McVeigh plotted the bombing enraged by the deaths of 80 Branch Davidian cult members in a siege by federal agents at Waco, Texas, two years before the bombing.

It presented evidence that he shopped for bomb components, rented the Ryder truck used in the bombing under a false name and had traces of explosives on his clothes when arrested after the blast. But it had no witness placing him in Oklahoma City on the day of the bombing.

The defence says authorities arrested the wrong man and that an unidentified leg found in the rubble of the Murrah building may have belonged to the bomber. It also took aim at the Fortiers' credibility, questioned the reliability of eyewitnesses and attacked results of forensic testing at the FBI's Washington crime laboratory, saying crucial evidence could have been contaminated.
